notes.definition: Graphite is a form of carbon with a giant covalent structure in which each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms, making layers of hexagonal rings with no covalent bonds between the layers. One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised.
explanation: In graphite, each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms. This produces flat layers made of hexagonal rings (rings of six carbon atoms), rather like a honeycomb or chicken wire. Within each layer the atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds, so each layer is a giant covalent structure. There are no covalent bonds between the layers; the layers are held together only by weak forces (weak intermolecular forces).

A carbon atom has four outer electrons. In graphite only three of these are used in covalent bonds. The fourth electron from each carbon atom is delocalised: it is free to move along the layer. In this way graphite is similar to metals, which also have delocalised electrons. Because these electrons can move through the structure and carry charge, graphite conducts electricity. The delocalised electrons also mean graphite conducts thermal energy.

Because the forces between the layers are weak, the layers can slide over each other easily. This makes graphite soft and slippery. It is why graphite is used in pencils (layers rub off onto the paper) and as a dry lubricant, for example in locks, where oil would attract dirt.

Even though graphite is soft, it has a very high melting point, similar to diamond. Melting requires the strong covalent bonds within the layers to be broken, not just the weak forces between them, and this needs a lot of energy. Graphite is also insoluble in water. Its high melting point and electrical conductivity make it useful for electrodes in electrolysis.

Make sure you can link each property to the right feature of the structure. Soft and slippery: weak forces between layers, so layers slide. High melting point: many strong covalent bonds within the layers must be broken. Conducts electricity: one delocalised electron per carbon atom, free to move through the layers. Compare graphite with diamond, where each carbon forms four bonds, so diamond is hard and has no delocalised electrons.
keyFacts: Graphite is a form of carbon with a giant covalent structure.
Each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms.
The atoms form layers of hexagonal rings.
There are no covalent bonds between the layers; only weak forces hold the layers together.
One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised.
Graphite conducts electricity and thermal energy because of its delocalised electrons, like metals.
Graphite is soft and slippery because the layers can slide over each other.
Graphite has a very high melting point because many strong covalent bonds must be broken.

keyTerms.definition: A form of carbon in which each atom is bonded to three others in layers of hexagonal rings, with one delocalised electron per atom.
A ring of six carbon atoms joined by covalent bonds; the repeating shape in graphite and graphene layers.
An electron not tied to one atom that can move through the structure; in graphite there is one per carbon atom.
A flat sheet of carbon atoms joined by strong covalent bonds in hexagonal rings.
A substance that reduces friction between surfaces; graphite works because its layers slide easily.

workedExamples.title: Explaining why graphite conducts
workedExamples.question: Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not.
steps: Graphite: each carbon forms 3 covalent bonds, so one of its 4 outer electrons is not used in bonding.
This electron is delocalised and can move through the layers, carrying charge.
Diamond: each carbon forms 4 covalent bonds, so all 4 outer electrons are used.
Diamond has no delocalised electrons, so it cannot carry charge.
workedExamples.answer: Graphite has one delocalised electron per carbon atom that can move and carry charge; in diamond all outer electrons are in bonds, so there are none.

workedExamples.title: Using data about bond and layer distances
workedExamples.question: The distance between carbon atoms within a graphite layer is 0.142 nm. The distance between layers is 0.335 nm. Calculate how many times larger the distance between layers is, and explain what this suggests.
steps: The layers are much further apart than atoms that are covalently bonded.
This suggests there are no covalent bonds between layers, only weak forces.
workedExamples.answer: About 2.36 times larger, which suggests the layers are held by weak forces rather than covalent bonds.

diagrams.title: Layers in graphite
diagrams.caption: Graphite is made of layers of hexagonal rings. Each carbon atom forms three strong covalent bonds within its layer. The layers are held together only by weak forces (dashed lines), so they can slide over each other.

diagrams.title: Delocalised electrons in a graphite layer
diagrams.caption: Top view of one layer. Each carbon atom (grey) forms three covalent bonds. Its fourth outer electron is delocalised (blue dots), free to move through the layer, so graphite conducts electricity.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think graphite has a low melting point because it is soft.
misconceptions.right: In fact graphite has a very high melting point. Softness comes from weak forces between layers, but melting requires breaking the strong covalent bonds within the layers.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the layers in graphite are held together by covalent bonds.
misconceptions.right: In fact there are no covalent bonds between the layers; only weak forces act between them, which is why they slide.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think graphite conducts because it contains ions, or because it is a metal.
misconceptions.right: In fact graphite is a non-metal with no ions. It conducts because one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say each carbon atom in graphite forms four bonds, as in diamond.
misconceptions.right: In fact each carbon atom in graphite forms three covalent bonds; the fourth outer electron is delocalised.

realWorld: Pencil 'lead' is graphite mixed with clay: layers slide off onto the paper to leave a mark.
Graphite is used as a dry lubricant in locks and machinery because its layers slide easily.
Graphite electrodes are used in electrolysis (for example in aluminium extraction) because graphite conducts electricity and has a very high melting point.
examTips: Use 'three covalent bonds' and 'layers of hexagonal rings' when describing graphite's structure.
For softness, say 'no covalent bonds between layers / weak forces between layers, so layers slide over each other'.
For conductivity, say 'one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised' and 'delocalised electrons can move and carry charge'.
Do not use weak forces between layers to explain the melting point: graphite's high melting point comes from breaking strong covalent bonds.
summary: Each carbon atom in graphite forms three covalent bonds.
Atoms form layers of hexagonal rings with no covalent bonds between layers.
Weak forces between layers let them slide, so graphite is soft and slippery.
One electron per carbon atom is delocalised, so graphite conducts electricity, like metals.
Graphite has a very high melting point because strong covalent bonds must be broken.
Uses include pencils, lubricants and electrodes.

questions.question: How many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form in graphite?
markScheme: 1 mark: 3
questions.explanation: Each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds. Four bonds per atom is diamond. Six is the number of atoms in each ring, not the bonds per atom.

questions.question: What shape are the rings of carbon atoms in graphite?
options: Pentagons
Squares
Hexagons
Triangles
markScheme: 1 mark: Hexagons
questions.explanation: Graphite layers are made of hexagonal rings of six carbon atoms.

questions.question: Why is graphite used in pencils?
options: Its layers slide off easily onto paper
It is very hard
It conducts electricity
It has a high melting point
markScheme: 1 mark: Its layers slide off easily onto paper
questions.explanation: Layers of graphite slide off and stick to paper. Hardness is wrong (graphite is soft); conductivity and melting point are true but not why it is used in pencils.

questions.question: Which property of graphite is similar to a metal?
options: It is very hard
It is a compound
It contains positive ions
It conducts electricity
markScheme: 1 mark: It conducts electricity
questions.explanation: Like metals, graphite has delocalised electrons and conducts electricity. It does not contain ions.

questions.question: What is between the layers in graphite?
options: Strong covalent bonds
Ionic bonds
Weak forces only, with no covalent bonds
Delocalised protons
markScheme: 1 mark: Weak forces only, with no covalent bonds
questions.explanation: There are no covalent bonds between the layers; weak forces hold them together, so the layers slide.

questions.question: Why does graphite conduct electricity?
options: It contains ions that move through the layers
One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised and can move through the structure
The layers slide and carry charge
Its covalent bonds are weak
markScheme: 1 mark: One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised and can move through the structure
questions.explanation: Each carbon atom uses three electrons in bonding; the fourth is delocalised and can carry charge. Graphite has no ions.

questions.question: Graphite is soft but has a very high melting point. Which explanation is correct?
options: Softness: weak forces between layers. High melting point: strong covalent bonds within layers must be broken
Softness: weak covalent bonds. High melting point: strong forces between layers
Softness: delocalised electrons. High melting point: ionic bonds
Softness: weak forces between molecules. High melting point: strong forces between molecules
markScheme: 1 mark: Softness: weak forces between layers. High melting point: strong covalent bonds within layers must be broken
questions.explanation: The two properties involve different parts of the structure. Sliding only overcomes weak forces between layers; melting needs strong covalent bonds to be broken.

questions.question: Which statement describes graphite correctly?
options: Each carbon atom is bonded to four others in a 3D network
Graphite is made of C₆₀ molecules
Graphite contains positive carbon ions and electrons
Each carbon atom is bonded to three others in layers
markScheme: 1 mark: Each carbon atom is bonded to three others in layers
questions.explanation: Graphite has layers in which each carbon is bonded to three others. Four bonds in 3D is diamond, and C₆₀ is a fullerene.

questions.question: Graphite is used for the electrodes in the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide at about 950 °C. Which two properties make it suitable?
options: Soft and slippery
Conducts electricity and has a very high melting point
Insoluble in water and very hard
Has weak forces between layers and conducts thermal energy
markScheme: 1 mark: Conducts electricity and has a very high melting point
questions.explanation: Electrodes must conduct electricity and must not melt at the high temperature of the electrolyte. Graphite does both.

questions.question: A student says: 'Graphite conducts electricity because its layers can slide.' What is the correct explanation?
options: Graphite conducts because it is a metal
Graphite conducts because it has ions between the layers
Graphite conducts because each carbon atom has one delocalised electron that can move through the structure
The student is correct
markScheme: 1 mark: Graphite conducts because each carbon atom has one delocalised electron that can move through the structure
questions.explanation: Sliding layers explain softness, not conductivity. Conductivity depends on mobile charged particles: the delocalised electrons.

questions.question: Graphite is used as a lubricant. What does a lubricant do?
options: Reduces friction between surfaces
Increases friction between surfaces
Conducts electricity between surfaces
Makes surfaces harder
markScheme: 1 mark: Reduces friction between surfaces
questions.explanation: Lubricants reduce friction. Graphite's layers slide over each other easily, so it reduces friction between moving parts.

questions.question: How many carbon atoms are in each ring in a graphite layer?
markScheme: 1 mark: 6
questions.explanation: The rings are hexagonal, so each contains six carbon atoms.

questions.question: A small piece of a graphite layer contains 500 carbon atoms. How many delocalised electrons does it have?
markScheme: 1 mark: 500
questions.explanation: Each carbon atom contributes one delocalised electron, so 500 atoms give 500 delocalised electrons.

questions.question:
In a graphite layer, each carbon atom forms 3 covalent bonds and each bond joins 2 carbon atoms.
Calculate the number of covalent bonds in a layer containing 1000 carbon atoms (ignore atoms at the edges).
markScheme: 1 mark: 1000 × 3 = 3000 (bond ends)
1 mark: ÷ 2 = 1500 bonds
questions.explanation: Each bond is counted twice if you multiply atoms by 3, so divide by 2: 1000 × 3 ÷ 2 = 1500.

questions.question:
In graphite, the distance between bonded carbon atoms within a layer is 0.142 nm and the distance between layers is 0.335 nm.
Calculate how many times greater the distance between layers is. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: 0.335 ÷ 0.142 = 2.359..., which is 2.36 to 3 significant figures. The large gap is consistent with weak forces rather than covalent bonds between layers.

questions.question: State the number of other carbon atoms each carbon atom is bonded to in graphite.
markScheme: 1 mark: three
questions.explanation: Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three others within its layer.

questions.question: Give one use of graphite.
markScheme: 1 mark: pencils / lubricant / electrodes
questions.explanation: Pencils and lubricants use the sliding layers; electrodes use conductivity and high melting point.

questions.question: Explain why graphite is soft and slippery.
markScheme: 1 mark: there are no covalent bonds between the layers / only weak forces between layers
1 mark: so the layers can slide over each other
questions.explanation: Two linked points: weak forces between layers, and therefore layers slide.

questions.question: Explain why graphite conducts electricity.
acceptedAnswers: one electron from each carbon delocalised
markScheme: 1 mark: one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised
1 mark: delocalised electrons can move (through the layers) and carry charge
questions.explanation: The answer must say why there are delocalised electrons and what they do.

questions.question: Explain why graphite has a very high melting point.
markScheme: 1 mark: many strong covalent bonds (within the layers)
1 mark: must be broken, which needs a lot of energy
questions.explanation: Melting graphite needs the covalent bonds in the layers to break, not just the weak forces between them.

questions.question: Explain why graphite is described as similar to metals, even though it is a non-metal.
acceptedAnswers: like the sea of electrons in metals
markScheme: 1 mark: graphite has delocalised electrons (like metals)
1 mark: so it conducts electricity (and thermal energy)
questions.explanation: The AQA specification highlights this similarity: graphite, like metals, has delocalised electrons.

questions.question: Compare the structure and bonding of graphite and diamond and use this to explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not.
markScheme: 1 mark: in graphite each carbon forms 3 covalent bonds (in layers); in diamond each carbon forms 4 covalent bonds
1 mark: in graphite one electron per carbon atom is delocalised and can carry charge
1 mark: in diamond all outer electrons are used in bonding, so there are no delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: The number of bonds per carbon atom decides whether an electron is left over to be delocalised.

questions.question: Describe the structure and bonding in graphite.
markScheme: Indicative content: form of carbon; giant covalent structure; each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds; with three other carbon atoms; forming hexagonal rings; arranged in flat layers; strong covalent bonds within layers; no covalent bonds between layers; weak forces between layers; one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised; delocalised electrons free to move along the layers.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear and detailed description including three bonds per carbon, hexagonal rings in layers, weak forces between layers and delocalised electrons.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct features, such as layers or covalent bonds, but incomplete or with errors.
questions.explanation: A complete description covers bonding within layers, between layers, and the delocalised electrons.

questions.question:
Graphite is used to make pencils, as a lubricant, and as electrodes.
Explain how the structure and bonding of graphite make it suitable for each of these uses.
markScheme: Indicative content: each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with other carbon atoms; layers of hexagonal rings; no covalent bonds between layers; weak forces between layers; layers slide over each other easily; graphite is soft and slippery; pencils: layers rub off onto paper leaving a mark; lubricant: layers slide, reducing friction between surfaces; does not need to be a liquid. Electrodes: one electron per carbon atom delocalised; delocalised electrons move and carry charge; so graphite conducts electricity; many strong covalent bonds within layers so very high melting point; does not melt at high temperatures of electrolysis.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): explains all three uses, each clearly linked to the correct feature of structure and bonding, with logical reasoning.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains two uses clearly, or all three with some errors or missing links.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about properties with little link to structure.
questions.explanation: Top answers match each use to the right feature: sliding layers (pencils, lubricant), delocalised electrons and strong covalent bonds (electrodes).

questions.question: Name the type of bond that joins the carbon atoms within a layer of graphite.
markScheme: 1 mark: (strong) covalent bonds
questions.explanation: Within each layer the carbon atoms share pairs of electrons, forming strong covalent bonds. Only weak forces act between layers.

questions.question: Graphite powder is sometimes used instead of oil to lubricate locks. Suggest one advantage of graphite and explain why graphite works as a lubricant.
markScheme: 1 mark: advantage, e.g. it is dry so does not attract dust or dirt / does not evaporate or drip
1 mark: the layers slide over each other easily because there are only weak forces between them
questions.explanation: A dry solid lubricant avoids sticky residues; it works because graphite layers slide easily.

questions.question: Where are the delocalised electrons in graphite able to move?
options: Only within one hexagonal ring
Through the layers of the structure
Only between the nucleus and inner shell
They cannot move
markScheme: 1 mark: Through the layers of the structure
questions.explanation: The delocalised electrons can move along the layers, which is why graphite conducts electricity.
